title: Introduce cancelable iterables and credential fallback chain across Python/TS/Go SDKs with minor version bumps
author: Aisha Kapoor
description: Motivation: Customers repeatedly ask for clearer cancellation and credential semantics when writing streaming consumers across languages. Current SDKs each have partial support (Py: cancel via iterator.close(), TS: AbortSignal in some layers, Go: Context usage inconsistent). This PR harmonizes three ergonomics areas: 1) a first-class cancelable async iterable/iterator contract in Python and TypeScript and a context-aware stream receiver/sink in Go; 2) a prioritized credential fallback chain that makes token providers composable and deterministic across SDKs; 3) small ergonomic factory helpers and typed error classes to reduce surface area for application code. What this does (summary): - Python: introduces CancelableAsyncIterator and AsyncIterableCursor that accept an explicit CancellationToken (backwards-compatible default omitted). Adds improved SessionFactory.with_credential_chain(...) helper, typed sdk.errors.StreamCanceled and sdk.errors.AuthUnavailable. Bumps py SDK minor to 0.18.0 in packaging metadata. - TypeScript: adds AsyncIterable<T> helpers that accept AbortSignal at creation and expose a cancel() helper for ergonomic callers. Unifies credential fallback chain into CredentialCascade class with well-documented priority: explicit credential > env > metadata > delegate-providers. Bumps TS SDK to 2.7.0. - Go: makes StreamReceiver and StreamSink context-aware (Context passed to Open/Recv/Close) and introduces CredentialChain type mirroring behavior of other SDKs. Bumps go SDK module to v1.6.1. Cross-SDK notes: the credential chain is pluggable and exposes a simple interface (GetToken(ctx)) implemented in each SDK so teams writing multi-language clients can rely on the same semantics. Backoff/retry defaults: tune the default retry/backoff profile used by streaming reconnects to be slightly more conservative (lower retry attempts, longer exponential base) to reduce cascading load during infra flaps. Telemetry: adds a small heartbeat event for long-lived streaming sessions to help identifying leaked consumers. Migration notes: default behavior is backwards compatible; customers only see change if they explicitly opt into the new helpers or pass cancellation tokens/AbortSignals/Contexts. Linear references: ENG-1456 (sdk streaming ergonomics), ENG-1902 (credential fallback implementation).

review_comments: Benji Martinez: Can we ensure the CancellationToken in Python is not GC-sensitive? Suggest adding an explicit close() path to the iterator — addressed in second commit where AsyncIterableCursor.close() performs a best-effort cleanup.
Aisha Kapoor (author): Added explicit close() and tests that validate weakref semantics. PTAL.
Liam O'Connell: TS side looks good but please add a small example showing AbortController usage with an external timeout — added under examples/ts and referenced in CHANGELOG.

María Fernández: Do the credential chain semantics match the existing environment precedence in our infra? Concern about metadata provider timing out during cold starts. Recommended small timeout on metadata provider — implemented with an optional timeout parameter and documented behavior.
Yuri Petrov: Go changes look clean but please ensure we don't break existing consumers that pass nil context — added a guard that uses context.Background() when ctx == nil.
CI Bot: Integration matrix failed on first run due to flaky network test in go. Re-ran and all checks passed.
Benji Martinez: Approve after minor nits fixed.
release_notes: Added cancelable async iterables across SDKs, a pluggable credential fallback chain, improved streaming retry defaults, and minor version bumps: Python 0.18.0, TypeScript 2.7.0, Go v1.6.1. Backwards compatible by default; see docs/sdk/cancellation.md and docs/sdk/credentials.md for migration steps.
notes: This PR intentionally groups small ergonomic changes across all three SDKs to keep the developer experience consistent. We kept changes minimal in serving logic and focused on client-side ergonomics and observability. No server-side contract changes.
